title: Soft recovery, KV eviction & backoff procedures (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This doc is an operational draft describing a low-risk, predictable soft-recovery pathway for the serving runtime when faced with memory pressure (OOM risk), kernel failures, or severe load spikes. It focuses on coordinated actions across KV cache management, request scheduling/backoff, and circuit breaker signals to avoid hard failures and to preserve tail-latency SLOs for high-priority traffic.

Scope and goals:
- Provide a deterministic, observable sequence to follow when a node or pool is experiencing memory pressure or OOMs.
- Prioritize user requests by tier (critical vs best-effort) during transient resource shortages.
- Minimize p95/p99 spikes by shifting behavior rather than hard rejecting traffic where possible.
- Ensure KV cache actions are reversible and designed to minimize quality regressions.
- Offer a short, executable on-call runbook plus programmatic heuristics for autoscaling and fallback.

Assumptions:
- Cluster autoscaler may take minutes to provision GPUs; soft recovery must operate on 10s–120s timescales.
- Models have multiple compatible variants (full-precision, quantized, CPU offload) registered in the model catalog.
- KV cache is per-model-shard with LRU-like eviction and rehydrate-on-read behavior.
- Requests are tagged with priority metadata and optionally user pinning/version.

Key failure modes addressed:
1) Gradual memory growth leading to OOM in the serving process.
2) Sudden memory spike from a single long context or large batch.
3) Kernel-level crash (CUDA kernel or driver) causing transient restarts.
4) Backpressure due to downstream queueing (storage, auth) amplifying memory usage.

High-level strategy:
1) Detect: aggressive metrics and short-window anomaly detectors (mem_used/busyness, evictions/sec, kernel_fail_count).
2) Contain: shift to soft-degrade mode (throttle concurrency per-core, limit max_seq_len, reduce batch depth).
3) Shrink working set: selective KV eviction, prefer evicting large prefixes and low-hit-rate keys.
4) Fallback: route lower-priority traffic to cheaper model variants or to regional pools.
5) Recover: graceful warmup/rehydrate and rollback when metrics return to baseline.

Detection and thresholds (suggested):
- Alert window: 30s rolling average memory utilization > 85% OR 5% rise in memory in last 20s -> enter soft-degrade diagnostics mode.
- Hardened action: memory > 92% sustained for 15s OR 3 OOMs in 5m -> apply aggressive containment and notify on-call.
- Kernel failure: any kernel restart (non-zero kernel_fail_count) triggers immediate mini-eviction and temporary reject of large-batch requests until a warmup guard passes.

KV cache actions (ordered, reversible):
A) Passive trimming: reduce per-request max_cached_prefix_size by 25% for new requests (cheap to apply).
B) Targeted eviction: evict keys with last_accessed > 2h OR per-key hit_rate < 0.01 over sliding 10m window. Preference: evict large KV entries first (size-weighted LRU).
C) Prefix compaction: if model supports consolidated KV layout, compact fragmented KV segments to reclaim overhead memory (safe path if compaction is lock-free).
D) Full purge (last resort): only on severe memory pressure (>95%) and with circuit breaker set; must trigger rehydrate-on-read and route high-priority traffic to warm nodes.

Notes on quality impact and mitigations:
- Evicting older low-hit keys should have minimal quality impact; track a comparative metric (embedding drift / reply-quality) for evicted prefixes to detect regressions.
- When prefix compaction or full purge is applied, proactively increase sampling of downstream evals on affected served prompts.

Request scheduling and backoff policy:
- Soft-degrade mode reduces concurrent_in_flight per GPU by 30-50% (configurable per model profile). This reduces KV working set and peak allocations.
- Prefer adaptive hedging for latency-sensitive requests: send a light-weight probe to a warm standby node after T_probe ms, cancel slower duplicate when faster responds.
- For best-effort requests, apply immediate exponential backoff with jitter: base=100ms, multiplier=2, max=5s, retries up to 3. Log retries with a trace id for analysis.
- For requests that exceed reduced max_seq_len, return structured error hinting at retriable truncation or offer a 'chunked' call pattern to clients.

Circuit breaker design and thresholds:
- Per-node and per-pool circuit breakers with states: CLOSED, SOFT_OPEN, HARD_OPEN.
- Transition to SOFT_OPEN when memory pressure + evictions/sec > threshold OR kernel fail rate spikes. In SOFT_OPEN: reject or reroute new large-batch and low-priority requests, enable KV passive trimming.
- Transition to HARD_OPEN after sustained SOFT_OPEN behavior for configured duration (default 45s) OR if an OOM occurs. HARD_OPEN: only accept critical traffic and force routing to other pools/variants.
- Circuit breaker must expose reasons and metric snapshots for debugging.

Runbook (on-call quick steps):
1) Pager: investigate node-level metrics (mem_used, evictions/sec, kernel_fail_count, concurrency).
2) If mem_used > 92%: trigger manual soft-restart of non-critical replicas, lower concurrency via /internal api, enable targeted eviction for affected shards.
3) If kernel failures present: cordon node, spin up replacement in same pool, route new traffic away until kernel_fail_count=0 for 3 intervals.
4) If OOM occurred: collect heap profiles, last 500 evicted keys list, and open an incident with tag oom/serving-runtime. Initiate full purge only with approval.
5) Monitor quality and rollback KV actions if quality regressions > configured tolerance.

Autoscaling and programmatic fallback recommendations:
- Prefer horizontal scale-up (add nodes) over vertical (bigger GPU SKU) when memory pressure is generally across many nodes.
- Autoscaler should be allowed to preemptively scale when queue depth > p95 expected processing time * target_capacity_margin.
- When autoscaler unavailable or slow, programmatic fallback should divert best-effort traffic to quantized/CPU-offload variants, and reserve capacity for critical traffic.

Observability and metrics to add (must be emitted):
- kv_evict_count, kv_evict_size_bytes, kv_hit_rate_by_tier, kv_rehydrate_count, kv_compaction_ops
- node_memory_bytes_total, node_memory_bytes_used, mem_growth_1m, mem_growth_30s
- kernel_restart_count, kernel_failure_reason_tags, kernel_restart_latency
- circuit_breaker_state (per-pool), circuit_breaker_reason, soft_open_timestamp
- request_retries_by_reason, hedged_probe_latency, rejected_by_cb_count

Testing and validation plan:
- Unit tests for eviction scoring logic, ensuring size-weighted LRU picks expected keys.
- Chaos tests: introduce synthetic memory pressure and validate that soft-degrade keeps p95 under target for priority traffic.
- Canary: enable passive trimming and targeted eviction on 5% of nodes for 48h, measure quality and tail latencies.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How aggressive should prefix compaction be before risking transient CPU spikes? (need benchmarks per-model)
- Backfill cost: rehydrating evicted prefixes for hot users could be expensive — we may need to persist hot-key hints to durable store to accelerate rehydrate.
- Should per-customer pinned models be exempt from aggressive eviction? (privacy vs stability trade-off)

Action items (owners):
- [Priya] implement targeted eviction scorer and expose kv_evict_size_bytes metric (ETA 2025-03-20).
- [Miguel] add circuit breaker state to tracer spans and implement SOFT_OPEN routing (ETA 2025-03-12).
- [Anika] run canary with passive trimming on gpu-pool-stable (ETA 2025-03-08).

Appendix: quick checklist for applying automated remediation (for operator automation)
- verify triggers: mem>85% && mem_growth_30s>3% -> enable passive trimming
- mem>92% || kernel_restart_count>1 -> targeted eviction + concurrency drop 40%
- OOM observed -> HARD_OPEN, route critical only, escalate, collect profiles

Notes to reviewers: this is a working doc. Major behavior changes need coordinated rollout with model-ops and product (especially any user-visible truncation or fallbacks). Please add comments inline or link PRs against the referenced github repo.
